channel.title: Romans — Stories of Scripture, Faith and Creation
channel.description: Illustrated films and carousels exploring Scripture, faithful service and the beauty of creation, by Landon Key.

item.title: William Tyndale
item.description:
From prison, William Tyndale asked for warm clothes, a lamp and a Hebrew Bible. His letter reveals practical needs behind the labor of bringing Scripture to others.

Beautiful Feet · A lamp, a coat and a Hebrew Bible

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Shi Meiyu (Mary Stone)
item.description:
Shi Meiyu translated medical lessons into Chinese so other nurses could care well. Her teaching and shared hospital work invite us to offer what we have learned.

Beautiful Feet · Words another nurse could use

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Rota Waitoa
item.description:
Rota Waitoa returned to study after becoming a pastor. His responsibilities and need for counsel invite humility about what faithful service still requires us to learn.

Beautiful Feet · The pastor who went back to learn

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Hilary of Poitiers
item.description:
Writing from exile, Hilary of Poitiers asked Christians to understand one another’s words about Christ. His patient explanations join doctrinal care with love.

Beautiful Feet · Hear what your brother means

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Dora Yu
item.description:
Dora Yu’s own testimony remembers her need to confess and receive grace. A Chinese Christian teacher’s account encourages honest repentance as we continue serving.

Beautiful Feet · The grace she wanted remembered

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Florens Radewijns and the prepared page
item.description:
Florens Radewijns prepared parchment, corrected books and received people seeking counsel. His shared household work invites gratitude for care behind another’s service.

Beautiful Feet · The prepared page and the open door

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Mary Magdalene
item.description:
Jesus met Mary Magdalene in her grief, called her by name and sent her with news of his resurrection. Her story directs sorrowing hearts toward the living Savior.

Beautiful Feet · Called by name and sent with hope

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Althea Brown Edmiston
item.description:
Althea Brown Edmiston learned the Bushoong language and prepared tools for reading it. Her work in Congo invites us to learn from the people we hope to serve.

Beautiful Feet · Learning from the people you serve

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Nerses and Armenian communities of care
item.description:
Nerses shared food and company with people pushed aside in fourth-century Armenia. His story considers personal welcome and the limits of organized provision.

Beautiful Feet · A place at the shared table

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Peter
item.description:
Peter denied Jesus and received mercy before strengthening others. His story includes restoration and later correction, encouraging honest repentance and care.

Beautiful Feet · Mercy for the one who would strengthen others

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Christiana Tsai, Mary Leaman and their friends
item.description:
Illness confined Christiana Tsai, while Mary Leaman and other friends shared life and ministry with her. Their fellowship shows belonging that severe limits cannot cancel.

Beautiful Feet · A place in Christ’s shared life

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Elida García de Falcón and Clotilde Falcón Náñez
item.description:
Elida García de Falcón translated by hand and Clotilde typed the pages. Their long partnership helped Spanish-speaking Methodist women share in the church’s work.

Beautiful Feet · The hands behind the finished page

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Michael Sattler
item.description:
Writing from prison, Michael Sattler urged patient love and asked for care for his wife. His letter remembers fellowship that includes the servant’s own needs.

Beautiful Feet · The love he asked them to keep

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Satoko Kitahara
item.description:
Satoko Kitahara joined the work of Tokyo’s Arinomachi community. Shared labor and illness shaped a story of learning from neighbors and receiving care too.

Beautiful Feet · She joined them in the work

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Eadburga
item.description:
Boniface thanked Eadburga for books and garments that strengthened him far from home. His letters preserve the practical kindness supporting missionary work.

Beautiful Feet · The books behind the journey

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: A sea full of wisdom
item.description:
Psalm 104 praises God’s wisdom in a sea full of creatures great and small. Notice the life beneath the surface and let wonder become worship of its Maker.

Clearly Seen · Psalm 104:24–26

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Keep sowing without knowing
item.description:
Ecclesiastes 11 pictures sowing when we cannot know which effort will prosper. Keep your promises and do faithful work while trusting God with its outcome.

Clearly Seen · Ecclesiastes 11:5–6

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: The God who names the stars
item.description:
Isaiah 40 turns weary eyes toward the Creator who names the stars and gives strength. Ask the God who never grows tired for help with your next step.

Clearly Seen · Isaiah 40:26–31

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What worry can’t give you
item.description:
Jesus points to birds and flowers as he speaks to anxious hearts in Matthew 6. Bring the Father your concerns and seek his kingdom in today’s next step.

Clearly Seen · Matthew 6:25–34

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Who holds the world together?
item.description:
God’s questions to Job draw attention to wisdom beyond our understanding. Hebrews 1 points to Christ upholding all things as we bring him our uncertainty.

Clearly Seen · Job 38:4–7 · Hebrews 1:3

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Your next breath
item.description:
Acts 17 names life and breath as gifts from the God who made the world. Let an ordinary breath lead to gratitude and love for someone near you today.

Clearly Seen · Acts 17:25

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Ampliatus
item.description:
Romans 16:8 calls Ampliatus beloved in the Lord without naming his work. Paul’s affection invites us to value a person’s presence as well as their achievements.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:8 · A person Paul called beloved.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Andronicus & Junia
item.description:
Paul honors Andronicus and Junia as fellow prisoners who were in Christ before him. Romans 16:7 remembers costly faith while leaving disputed wording open to study.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:7 · Their faith came before his.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Apelles
item.description:
Romans 16:10 honors Apelles as approved in Christ without describing his trial. Remember faithful people with care for the parts of their lives we do not know.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:10 · A faithful life. An untold test.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Asyncritus and the brothers with them
item.description:
Romans 16:14 greets five named believers and the brothers with them. Their shared life invites attention to people known personally within a smaller circle.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:14 · Five names. And others with them.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: The churches greeting the church
item.description:
The churches of Christ send greetings beyond their own communities in Romans 16:16. Local belonging opens toward a wider fellowship and the hope of the nations.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:16 · Your church is part of a larger family.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Ebed-melech
item.description:
Ebed-melech spoke up for Jeremiah and brought cloth to protect him during rescue. Jeremiah 38–39 remembers courageous help attentive to a suffering person’s needs.

The Names You Almost Missed · Jeremiah 38:7–13; 39:15–18 · He spoke up, then brought the cloth.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Epaenetus
item.description:
Paul remembers Epaenetus as beloved and the first convert to Christ in Asia. Romans 16:5 invites us to honor early steps of faith and those who encourage them.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:5 · Remember the first steps.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Erastus
item.description:
Romans 16:23 names Erastus, described as city treasurer, among the greeting companions. Consider civic service while keeping the debated Corinth inscription distinct.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:23 · A public role. A personal greeting.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Gaius
item.description:
Paul names Gaius as host to him and the whole church in Romans 16:23. His welcome invites gratitude for people who make room for others to belong.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:23 · Welcome that reached a church.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Herodion
item.description:
Paul calls Herodion his kinsman in Romans 16:11. Honor the relationship the greeting gives us while leaving its precise family connection unclaimed.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:11 · A kinship Paul remembered.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Those of Aristobulus
item.description:
Paul greets the people associated with Aristobulus in Romans 16:10. A household label points to real people whose individual names we have not received.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:10 · The people behind a household name.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Those in the Lord of Narcissus
item.description:
Romans 16:11 greets those in the Lord associated with Narcissus. Their shared household connection helps us consider personal welcome and belonging in Christ.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:11 · Another household. A deeper belonging.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Jason
item.description:
Romans 16:21 names Jason among those sending greetings. Compare the costly welcome of Acts 17 while recognizing that the two men are not explicitly identified.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:21 · A name that invites a careful connection.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Lucius
item.description:
Lucius sends greetings in Romans 16:21 alongside Paul’s companions. Notice his participation while keeping possible links to Lucius of Cyrene distinct from what is known.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:21 · A greeting from Lucius, too.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Lydia
item.description:
The Lord opened Lydia’s heart as she listened at Philippi, and she welcomed Paul’s companions into her home. Acts 16 connects received grace with practical hospitality.

The Names You Almost Missed · Acts 16:14–15, 40 · An opened heart, a welcoming home.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Mary
item.description:
Romans 16:6 names Mary and honors her hard work for the church. Her unnamed tasks invite us to thank real people without inventing details about their service.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:6 · We don’t have her task list. Paul gives us her name.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Rufus’s mother
item.description:
Paul remembers Rufus’s mother as a mother to him too. Romans 16:13 honors the lasting weight of personal care, though her name is absent from our reading.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:13 · Paul remembered her motherly care.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Nereus’s sister
item.description:
Nereus’s sister is included in Romans 16:15 without her name being recorded. Her greeting invites us to value being known among our people and by Christ.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:15 · Her name is missing. Her place is not.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Onesiphorus
item.description:
Onesiphorus searched earnestly for Paul in Rome and was unashamed of his chains. Second Timothy remembers friendship that made the effort to find and refresh him.

The Names You Almost Missed · 2 Timothy 1:16–18; 4:19 · He searched until he found his friend.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Persis
item.description:
Romans 16:12 remembers Persis as beloved and hardworking in the Lord. Her greeting invites gratitude that values a person’s friendship as well as their service.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:12 · Her work mattered. So did she.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Phoebe
item.description:
Phoebe helped many people, including Paul. In Romans 16:1–2, he asks the church to welcome and assist her, inviting care to travel both ways.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:1–2 · Who helps the helper?

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Priscilla & Aquila
item.description:
Shared work, patient teaching and a church in their house connect Priscilla and Aquila’s story. Acts 18 and Romans 16 honor their costly gospel partnership.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:3–5 · They made room for the church.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Quartus
item.description:
Romans 16:23 calls Quartus our brother, with no title or list of achievements. His greeting gives Christian belonging a name worth remembering.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:23 · One word of honor: our brother.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Rufus
item.description:
Paul greets Rufus as chosen in the Lord and remembers his mother’s care. Romans 16:13 invites reflection on belonging in Christ without ranking believers.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:13 · A name held in Christ.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Philologus and the saints with them
item.description:
Romans 16:15 includes a wider circle alongside Philologus and the other names. People without an individual line still belong among God’s beloved people.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:15 · A greeting large enough to include them.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Sosipater
item.description:
Sosipater has a place among Paul’s greeting companions in Romans 16:21. Honor his fellowship while leaving the proposed connection with Sopater of Berea open.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:21 · A person beyond a possible match.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Stachys
item.description:
Paul names Stachys as beloved beside Urbanus in Romans 16:9. Each person deserves attention, even when their greetings share a single sentence.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:9 · The other name in the sentence.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Tabitha / Dorcas
item.description:
The widows of Joppa remembered garments Tabitha had made. Acts 9 connects a disciple’s useful skill, her neighbors’ grief and the mercy that restored her life.

The Names You Almost Missed · Acts 9:36–43 · The clothes her neighbors remembered.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Tertius
item.description:
Tertius, who wrote Romans, adds his own greeting in the Lord. His words invite us to recognize the careful work that helps a message reach other people.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:22 · The hand behind the letter speaks.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Timothy
item.description:
Romans 16 names Timothy as Paul’s fellow worker. Other letters show the genuine concern and proven service behind this greeting from a trusted companion.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:21 · A trusted coworker who cared.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Tryphaena & Tryphosa
item.description:
Paul honors Tryphaena and Tryphosa as workers in the Lord. Romans 16:12 recognizes shared service while leaving their tasks and family connection unrecorded.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:12 · Two names. Work in the Lord.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Tychicus
item.description:
Tychicus carried trustworthy news to encourage believers’ hearts. Ephesians and Colossians show how faithful communication helped churches care across distance.

The Names You Almost Missed · Ephesians 6:21–22 · Trusted with news that encouraged hearts.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: Urbanus
item.description:
Romans 16:9 names Urbanus as a fellow worker in Christ. His greeting invites us to include the people whose contributions make ministry shared work.

The Names You Almost Missed · Romans 16:9 · Our fellow worker in Christ.

Explore the carousel and read the story

item.title: What is shaping the choice I want to make?
item.description:
Romans 12:2 connects wise decisions with a renewed mind. Scripture helps us examine desires for status or comfort and learn what pleases God.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:2

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What can I pray when my heart won’t settle?
item.description:
Romans 15:13 gives a restless heart words to pray. Ask the God of hope for joy and peace as you trust him, through the Holy Spirit’s power.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 15:12–13

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Could an ordinary workday become gospel partnership?
item.description:
Paul’s shared trade with Priscilla and Aquila grew into gospel partnership. Acts 18 and Romans 16 invite faithfulness to the people already near us.

Romans, illustrated · Acts 18:1–3; Romans 16:3–5

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What does adoption add to forgiveness?
item.description:
Romans 8 describes the Spirit of adoption and belonging as God’s children. That family hope holds through suffering on the way to glory with Christ.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:15–17

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Where does knowing God’s will begin?
item.description:
Romans 12 begins discernment with God’s mercies. Offering your life to him gives a place to begin as you consider work, opportunities and people affected.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:1–2

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: How can I begin when I do not know my gift?
item.description:
You can begin serving before you can name your spiritual gift. Romans 12 invites practical help, wise counsel and learning alongside your church.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:3-8

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Who has the final word over my guilt?
item.description:
Romans 8 answers returning guilt with Christ’s death, resurrection and intercession. Those God has justified can rest in the Savior who speaks for them.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:1, 33–34

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Who could encourage an apostle?
item.description:
In Romans 1, Paul expects ordinary believers to encourage his faith too. Christian service includes receiving strength as well as offering it.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 1:11–12

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Can I choose faithfully while I still feel uncertain?
item.description:
Romans 12 invites thoughtful discernment as God renews our minds. Scripture, prayer and wise counsel can guide a faithful step amid uncertainty.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:2

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: How do I fight sin without relying on myself?
item.description:
Romans 8 calls believers to put sinful deeds to death by the Spirit. Bring ordinary temptations to God and depend on his help as you turn from sin.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:9–15

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Can God forgive the sin I still remember?
item.description:
Romans 4 speaks of real forgiveness for real guilt. A painful memory can be brought honestly to God while faith rests in his mercy through Christ.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 4:5–8

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What matters more than winning a food argument?
item.description:
Romans 14 asks how our choices affect another believer’s conscience. Love pursues peace and builds up the person for whom Christ died.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 14:1–4, 15–19

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why would I help someone who hurt me?
item.description:
Romans 12 calls us to meet an enemy’s real need. Christ’s mercy can shape a wise act of kindness without buying an apology or pretending trust is restored.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:20–21; 5:8–10

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why did Paul want to preach the gospel to Christians?
item.description:
Paul wanted to preach the gospel to believers in Rome. Romans 1 shows why familiar good news about Christ continues to nourish and deepen Christian faith.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 1:8, 15–17

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why do I feel less gifted than everyone else?
item.description:
Romans 12:3–8 helps us receive our different gifts with humility. God’s grace gives you a place to serve without becoming the person beside you.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:3-8

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why does Paul call grace a gift?
item.description:
Romans 3–4 contrasts earned wages with God’s gift of righteousness. Faith receives what Christ has secured, leaving us grateful and without grounds to boast.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 3:24–28; 4:4–5

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Does Christian hope mean I should stop crying?
item.description:
Romans 8 gives grieving believers resurrection hope while acknowledging their groaning. Romans 12 calls us to share their tears and remain beside them.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:23–25; 12:15

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: If I give up revenge, does the wrong still matter?
item.description:
Romans 12–13 distinguishes personal revenge from proper accountability. You can seek protection and tell the truth while entrusting final judgment to God.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:18–19; 13:3–4

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why do I know better, yet still sin?
item.description:
Romans 7 shows how God’s good law exposes sin without supplying its cure. Romans 8 directs our hope for rescue to what God has done through Christ.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 7:7–25; 8:1–4

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: How can I help after the first visit?
item.description:
Shared sorrow continues through prayer and practical care. Romans 12 encourages specific offers of help and patient attention after the first visit.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:9,12–13,15

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: How far does God’s love reach?
item.description:
Romans connects God’s mercy with the gospel reaching the nations. Prayer, giving and shared sending let a local church take part in that purpose.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 1:5–7; 15:8–12,20–24; 16:25–27

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: How do I know God loves me when life hurts?
item.description:
Christ’s death shows God’s love for sinners, and suffering cannot separate his people from that love. Romans 5 and 8 invite hurting hearts to draw near.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 5:6–11; 8:35–39

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why does God’s love bring us together?
item.description:
Romans 12 and 15 describe life together in Christ: receiving help, strengthening others and welcoming people with the patience his mercy has shown us.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:4–5; 15:1–7

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Do I have to say yes to every need?
item.description:
Romans 12 pictures a body whose members have different gifts. Share the work, receive help and serve faithfully without trying to meet every need yourself.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:3-8

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What about the harm I have caused?
item.description:
God’s mercy gives courage to admit harm, listen and change. Romans 12 calls us to pursue peace while respecting another person’s time and boundaries.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:9, 17–18; 13:8–10

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why Romans ends with names
item.description:
Phoebe, Priscilla, Aquila and Mary help us see the people living out the gospel in Romans 16. Their greetings invite gratitude for faithful people nearby.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 16:1–13

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What is God’s patience inviting us to do?
item.description:
Romans 2:4 warns against taking God’s kindness for granted. His patience invites us to name the sin we excuse and turn to him for mercy.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 2:4

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Can I have peace with God on an anxious day?
item.description:
Romans 5:1–2 grounds peace with God in what Christ has secured. You can bring him an anxious mind while standing in the grace he has given you.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 5:1–2

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: If I am free, why am I still tempted?
item.description:
Romans 6 distinguishes temptation’s presence from sin’s mastery. Those united to Christ can remember their new life and offer their words and actions to God.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 6:1–14

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What can a quiet conversation do?
item.description:
Priscilla and Aquila helped Apollos understand God’s way more accurately. Their patient conversation invites us to open Scripture with someone who needs help.

Romans, illustrated · Acts 18:24–28; Romans 16:3

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Does evil get the last word?
item.description:
Romans 16 promises that the God of peace will defeat Satan. A troubled church can hold to the gospel and choose what is good while evil still threatens.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 16:17–20

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What should a grafted branch remember?
item.description:
Romans 11 pictures Gentile believers as grafted olive branches. Dependence on God’s mercy calls for gratitude and humility toward Jewish people.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 11:17–22

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What does “good” mean?
item.description:
Romans 8:28–30 connects God’s promise of good with becoming like Christ. Read the promise beside its purpose when suffering makes the future hard to see.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:28–30

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: Why does getting even leave me worse off?
item.description:
A cruel reply can carry someone else’s hurt further. Romans 12 calls us to truthful words shaped by mercy and to overcome evil with good.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:17–18,21

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: What if I don’t know what to say to someone grieving?
item.description:
Romans 12:15 invites us to stay beside people who grieve. Listening, shared silence and patient company can express love when an explanation cannot help.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 12:9–10,15

Watch the film and read the narration

item.title: When words fail
item.description:
Romans 8:26–27 speaks to weakness in prayer: the Spirit intercedes according to God’s will. Bring God the words you have, even when they feel unfinished.

Romans, illustrated · Romans 8:26–27

Watch the film and read the narration
